title: How Organ Donation Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss organ donation: the first living-donor kidney transplant between twins Richard and Ronald Herrick in 1954, earlier and odd transplant history, the waiting list statistics from UNOS (checked live during the show), which organs can come from living versus deceased donors, organ regeneration of the liver, religious objections (Shinto, Amish, Jehovah's Witnesses, Romani), registering through the DMV and Georgia's seven-dollar incentive, brain death versus cardiac death procurement rules including the sixty-five-second rule and the apnea test, organ procurement organizations, UNOS, SRTR and OPTN, organ transport, post-transplant lifestyle expectations, the black market in organs and kidney theft, and a listener mail story about a bookstore thief's journal.

segments.title: Opening banter and organ donation introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about kidneys and livers, then introduce organ donation as the topic.

segments.title: History of transplants and the 1954 twin kidney transplant
segments.summary: The first successful living-to-living organ donation was a kidney from Ronald Herrick to his dying twin Richard in 1954, with low rejection risk due to twin genetics. Earlier and odd transplant attempts are mentioned, and the hosts note that more than half a million transplants have been performed.

segments.title: Live waiting list statistics from UNOS
segments.summary: The hosts read up-to-the-minute waiting list numbers from UNOS: about 105,000 people waiting for organs and 83,012 for kidneys, and plan to recheck later.

segments.title: What organs are and organ reserve capacity
segments.summary: Chuck explains organs as systems of cells and tissues, noting their reserve capacity and that corneas do not deteriorate with age like other organs. Organs do deteriorate with age, and wait times for organs are discussed, including a median wait of 6.7 years for heart-lung combinations.

segments.title: Living versus deceased donation and the liver
segments.summary: Organs can come from living or deceased donors; hearts generally come only from deceased donors. The liver can regenerate, so a portion can be donated, including to children, and it grows back to full size.

segments.title: Religious objections and donor eligibility
segments.summary: Exceptions to donation are discussed, including HIV and certain infections, and religious views from Shinto, Amish, Romani, and Jehovah's Witnesses, which are explained.

segments.title: Registering as a donor and Georgia's seven-dollar incentive
segments.summary: Registration is done at the DMV. Georgia once paid seven dollars off driver's licenses for donor sign-ups, which made donor rates hard to trust; the program stopped in 2005 because compensation for organs is illegal.

segments.title: Brain death versus cardiac death and procurement rules
segments.summary: Deceased donation happens by brain death or cardiac death. Cardiac death lacks laws; a five-minute wait was established, then a Colorado doctor's sixty-five-second rule, which was challenged in an unsuccessful lawsuit. Brain death is defined by tests including an apnea test, and the ventilator blurs the line between life and death. A 2008 white paper is mentioned.

segments.title: Organ procurement organizations and related networks
segments.summary: Organ procurement organizations are federally designated nonprofits that handle awareness, recruitment, evaluation, removal, and transport, and talk to families. Hospitals must notify them of deaths. UNOS, SRTR, and OPTN are described, and the advice to put donor wishes in a living will is given.

segments.title: Organ transport and post-transplant expectations
segments.summary: Organs are flown in coolers between cities. Living donors get some consideration on waiting lists, and insurance may penalize former donors. Recipients are expected to live healthily, and recipients typically pay donor travel costs.

segments.title: Organ black market and kidney theft
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the illegal organ trade, mostly in poor countries, including a 2003 South African case with Brazilian sellers, Indian villagers paid around $800, and Israeli brokers in Turkey. A Delhi kidney theft case is described. A 2000 New York case involved Biomedical Tissue Services, which sold tissue including from Alistair Cook.

segments.title: Listener mail: bookstore thief's journal
segments.summary: Sarah writes about a bookstore that received a journal from a long-time thief who logged every book stolen over twenty years; the thief was from a prominent local family and the matter was settled out of court.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts encourage listeners to email and mention further resources on how stuff works, then sign off.
